specStatements.text: Scalar quantities have magnitude only.
Vector quantities have magnitude and an associated direction.
A vector quantity may be represented by an arrow. The length of the arrow represents the magnitude, and the direction of the arrow the direction of the vector quantity.
A force is a push or pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object. All forces between objects are either:
• contact forces – the objects are physically touching
• non-contact forces – the objects are physically separated.
Examples of contact forces include friction, air resistance, tension and normal contact force.
Examples of non-contact forces are gravitational force, electrostatic force and magnetic force.
Force is a vector quantity.
Students should be able to describe the interaction between pairs of objects which produce a force on each object. The forces to be represented as vectors.
Weight is the force acting on an object due to gravity. The force of gravity close to the Earth is due to the gravitational field around the Earth.
The weight of an object depends on the gravitational field strength at the point where the object is.
The weight of an object can be calculated using the equation:
weight = mass × gravitational field strength
[W = m g]
weight, W, in newtons, N
mass, m, in kilograms, kg
gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg (In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given.)
The weight of an object may be considered to act at a single point referred to as the object’s ‘centre of mass’.
The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional.
Weight is measured using a calibrated spring-balance (a newtonmeter).
A number of forces acting on an object may be replaced by a single force that has the same effect as all the original forces acting together. This single force is called the resultant force.
Students should be able to calculate the resultant of two forces that act in a straight line.
(HT only) Students should be able to:
• describe examples of the forces acting on an isolated object or system
• use free body diagrams to describe qualitatively examples where several forces lead to a resultant force on an object, including balanced forces when the resultant force is zero.
(HT only) A single force can be resolved into two components acting at right angles to each other. The two component forces together have the same effect as the single force.

(HT only) Students should be able to use vector diagrams to illustrate resolution of forces, equilibrium situations and determine the resultant of two forces, to include both magnitude and direction (scale drawings only).

scopeNotes.statement: gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg (In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given.)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item in this material asks a student to recall a value of gravitational field strength, and no item can be answered only by someone who has memorised one. Every calculation states the value of g inside the stem in N/kg, and the comparison items that set one location against another either state both values of g or are answered by proportional reasoning from the numbers supplied. Where the Moon or another planet appears, the stem gives the field strength there rather than expecting it to be known.

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) Students should be able to use vector diagrams to illustrate resolution of forces, equilibrium situations and determine the resultant of two forces, to include both magnitude and direction (scale drawings only).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Resultants and components of forces that are not in a straight line are treated as scale-drawing work throughout. No item requires a trigonometric ratio or Pythagoras' theorem to be quoted or applied: the vector-diagram items are answered by describing the construction (drawing the arrows to scale, head to tail, and measuring the closing arrow with a ruler and protractor), or by reading a value from a stated scale. The 3-4-5 figures used are ones a correctly drawn scale diagram would deliver by measurement, and the correct option never depends on calculating them.

concepts.definition: A quantity that has magnitude only. A scalar is fully described by a size and a unit, with no direction attached to it. Mass, speed, distance, energy and time are scalars.
A quantity that has magnitude and an associated direction. A vector is only fully described when both are given. Force, weight, velocity, displacement and acceleration are vectors.

The representation of a vector quantity by an arrow drawn on a diagram. The length of the arrow represents the magnitude of the vector, and the direction the arrow points represents the direction of the vector quantity.

A push or pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object. A force is not something an object stores or owns; it exists only while two objects interact, and it is measured in newtons.
A force between two objects that are physically touching. Friction, air resistance, tension and the normal contact force are contact forces.
A force between two objects that are physically separated. Gravitational force, electrostatic force and magnetic force are non-contact forces.
A contact force that acts between two surfaces that are touching, acting along the surfaces and opposing the relative motion, or attempted motion, between them.
A contact force acting on an object moving through air. The object is physically touching the particles of the air, which is why it is classed as a contact force.
A contact force transmitted along a stretched rope, string, cable or spring, pulling on the objects attached at each end of it.
The contact force exerted by a surface on an object that is touching it, acting at right angles (normal) to that surface.
A non-contact force of attraction between two objects that have mass. It acts even though the objects are physically separated, for example between the Earth and an object above its surface.
A non-contact force between electrically charged objects. Like charges repel and opposite charges attract, and the force acts across the space between the charged objects.
A non-contact force between magnets, or between a magnet and a magnetic material, which acts across the gap between them without the objects touching.
The two forces produced when two objects interact. Each object exerts a force on the other, the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, and each force acts on a different object.

The force acting on an object due to gravity, measured in newtons, N. Close to the Earth it is due to the gravitational field around the Earth, and it is calculated from weight = mass × gravitational field strength.

The quantity, symbol g, measured in newtons per kilogram, N/kg, that describes the strength of a gravitational field at a point. The weight of an object depends on the gravitational field strength at the point where the object is.

The quantity of matter in an object, symbol m, measured in kilograms, kg. Mass is a scalar quantity and it does not change when the object is moved to a place with a different gravitational field strength.

The single point at which the weight of an object may be considered to act. Treating the weight as one force acting at this point allows an object to be handled as though all of its mass were concentrated there.

A relationship in which one quantity is a fixed multiple of another, so that multiplying one by a number multiplies the other by the same number, and a graph of one against the other is a straight line through the origin. The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional.
A calibrated spring-balance used to measure weight in newtons. The spring extends more as the force pulling on it increases, and the scale is marked so that the reading gives the weight directly.
The single force that has the same effect as all of the original forces acting on an object together. A number of forces acting on an object may always be replaced by this one force.

A diagram showing a single isolated object or system on its own, with every force acting on that object drawn as an arrow from it. It is used to describe qualitatively how several forces combine to give a resultant force.
Forces on an object that combine to give a resultant force of zero. The individual forces are still acting, but they have no overall effect on the motion of the object.
Replacing a single force by two component forces acting at right angles to each other. The two component forces together have the same effect as the single force they replace.
The situation in which the forces acting on an object are balanced, so the resultant force is zero. On a scale vector diagram the arrows representing the forces form a closed shape.

misconceptions.question: Is speed a vector quantity because a moving object is always going somewhere?
misconceptions.correct: Speed is a scalar: it has magnitude only. Velocity is the vector, because velocity states a speed together with a direction.
misconceptions.misconception: Any quantity that describes something moving must be a vector, so speed counts as a vector.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Motion feels directional, so students attach direction to every quantity that describes it. The pair speed/velocity is also used interchangeably in everyday speech, which hides the distinction the specification draws.
misconceptions.correction: Test the quantity, not the situation: ask whether the number alone fully describes it. '30 m/s' is a complete speed but an incomplete velocity, because a velocity is not fixed until a direction such as 'north' is added.

misconceptions.question: On a force diagram, does the length of an arrow matter?
misconceptions.correct: The length of the arrow represents the magnitude of the vector, so a longer arrow means a larger force. The direction the arrow points represents the direction of the force.
misconceptions.misconception: The arrow only shows which way the force acts, so its length can be drawn to whatever size looks neat.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In sketches used in other subjects an arrow is purely a pointer, and students carry that habit into physics diagrams where the arrow is a scale representation.
misconceptions.correction: Read a force arrow as carrying two pieces of information at once. Drawing a 20 N force twice as long as a 10 N force is not decoration; it is the part of the diagram that records the magnitude.

misconceptions.question: Does a stationary book resting on a table have a force in it?
misconceptions.correct: A force is a push or pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object. The book does not contain force; it experiences forces from the Earth and from the table.
misconceptions.misconception: Objects contain or store force, and heavy objects contain more force than light ones.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday phrases such as 'the force of the blow' or 'it has a lot of force' treat force as a substance an object carries, rather than as an interaction between two objects.
misconceptions.correction: Always finish the sentence: which other object is exerting this force? If no second object can be named, what is being described is not a force.

misconceptions.question: Is the gravitational force on a falling ball a contact force, because the ball is in the air?
misconceptions.correct: It is a non-contact force. Gravitational force acts between the Earth and the ball while they are physically separated.
misconceptions.misconception: A force is a contact force whenever the two objects are anywhere near each other, or whenever the object is touching something.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students classify by what is visible around the object rather than by which two objects the force acts between. Because a falling ball touches air, it looks as though contact is involved.
misconceptions.correction: Name the two objects the force acts between first, then ask whether those two objects are touching. For weight the pair is the Earth and the object, and they are physically separated.

misconceptions.question: Air resistance acts on a skydiver who is not touching anything solid, so is it a non-contact force?
misconceptions.correct: Air resistance is a contact force. The skydiver is physically touching the particles of the air that the force acts between.
misconceptions.misconception: Air resistance is a non-contact force because the falling object is not touching the ground or any solid surface.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Air is invisible and is not thought of as an object, so students judge the skydiver to be touching nothing at all.
misconceptions.correction: Treat air as matter that can be touched. Contact with the particles of the air is real contact, which is why the specification lists air resistance among the contact forces.

misconceptions.question: A magnet is stuck to a fridge door. Is the magnetic force now a contact force?
misconceptions.correct: Magnetic force is a non-contact force. It acts across a gap and does not stop being a non-contact force when the objects happen to be touching.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnetic force becomes a contact force once the magnet and the metal are touching each other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The classification is read off the final position of the objects rather than off the nature of the force, and a magnet held against a fridge does touch it.
misconceptions.correction: Ask whether the force can act with a gap between the objects. Magnetic, electrostatic and gravitational forces all can, so they are non-contact forces however close the objects end up.

misconceptions.question: Is it enough to say that a force of 50 N acts on a crate?
misconceptions.correct: No. Force is a vector quantity, so a full description gives the magnitude and the direction, for example 50 N vertically downwards.
misconceptions.misconception: A force is completely described by its size in newtons, and the direction is extra detail that can be left out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Numerical answers are rewarded in most calculations, so students learn to stop once a number and a unit have been written down.
misconceptions.correction: Check every force answer for two parts. If the answer would be equally true for a push to the left and a push to the right, the direction is still missing.

misconceptions.question: A lorry collides with a small car. Does the lorry exert a bigger force on the car than the car exerts on the lorry?
misconceptions.correct: No. The two objects interact, and each exerts a force on the other that is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
misconceptions.misconception: The bigger or faster object pushes harder, so the force it exerts is larger than the force it receives.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The damage to the two vehicles is very different, and students reasonably read the unequal damage as evidence of unequal forces rather than of unequal mass.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the force from its effect. The forces of an interaction pair are equal in magnitude; the car is damaged more because the same size of force acts on a much smaller mass.

misconceptions.question: If the forces in an interaction pair are equal and opposite, why does anything ever move?
misconceptions.correct: The two forces act on two different objects, so they can never cancel each other out. Only forces acting on the same object combine to give a resultant.
misconceptions.misconception: The two forces of an interaction pair act on the same object, so they always cancel and nothing can accelerate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balanced forces on one object and the two forces of an interaction pair look identical when drawn as a pair of opposing arrows, and students merge the two ideas.
misconceptions.correction: Label every arrow with the object it acts on. An interaction pair always has one arrow on each of the two objects; balanced forces always have both arrows on the same object.

misconceptions.question: A bag of sugar is labelled 1 kg. Is that its weight?
misconceptions.correct: No, that is its mass. Weight is the force acting on the bag due to gravity, and weight is measured in newtons, N.
misconceptions.misconception: Weight and mass are the same quantity, and weight can be given in kilograms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language calls the reading on kitchen scales a weight, and those scales are marked in kilograms, so the two quantities arrive already merged.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the units apart and the quantities stay apart: mass, m, in kilograms, kg; weight, W, in newtons, N. Weight is a force and mass is not.

misconceptions.question: An astronaut takes a toolbox to the Moon. What happens to its mass and its weight?
misconceptions.correct: The mass is unchanged, because mass does not depend on location. The weight is smaller, because the gravitational field strength at the Moon's surface is smaller than at the Earth's surface.
misconceptions.misconception: Both the mass and the weight of the toolbox get smaller on the Moon, because there is less gravity there.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Because mass and weight are already confused, anything that reduces one is assumed to reduce the other, and 'less gravity on the Moon' is a familiar fact.
misconceptions.correction: Work through W = m g. Moving the toolbox changes g only. The m in the equation is the same number on the Moon as on the Earth, so only W changes.

misconceptions.question: What does the g in W = m g stand for?
misconceptions.correct: It is the gravitational field strength at the point where the object is, measured in newtons per kilogram, N/kg.
misconceptions.misconception: The g is the force of gravity acting on the object, measured in newtons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbol g is spoken aloud as 'gravity', and a quantity that appears in a force equation is assumed to be a force itself.
misconceptions.correction: Read the unit. N/kg means newtons per kilogram of mass, so g tells you how much weight each kilogram gets. The force itself is W, the answer, not g.

misconceptions.question: To find the mass of an object from its weight, what do you do with g?
misconceptions.correct: Divide the weight by the gravitational field strength, because W = m g rearranges to m = W ÷ g.
misconceptions.misconception: Multiply the weight by g, because the equation contains a multiplication sign.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is remembered as a string of symbols rather than as a relationship, so the operation written in it is repeated whichever quantity is being found.
misconceptions.correction: Rearrange before substituting. Start from W = m g, isolate the quantity asked for, and only then put the numbers in; a mass in kilograms should come out smaller than the weight in newtons wherever g is greater than 1 N/kg.

misconceptions.question: Where does the weight of an object act?
misconceptions.correct: The weight may be considered to act at a single point called the centre of mass of the object.
misconceptions.misconception: Weight acts at the point where the object touches the ground, because that is where it presses down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The visible effect of weight is felt at the surface an object rests on, so students place the force there instead of at the centre of mass.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish the two forces at a contact. The push on the ground is the contact force between the object and the surface; the weight is the pull of gravity on the whole object, drawn from its centre of mass.

misconceptions.question: The mass of an object is trebled. What happens to its weight in the same field?
misconceptions.correct: The weight is also trebled. Weight and mass are directly proportional, so multiplying the mass by three multiplies the weight by three.
misconceptions.misconception: The weight simply goes up by some amount, or goes up by adding the same number again.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Directly proportional' is read as a vague statement that one quantity increases with the other, rather than as a fixed multiplying relationship.
misconceptions.correction: Test proportionality with a ratio, not a difference. If W ÷ m gives the same value for every object in the same field, the two quantities are directly proportional, and the graph is a straight line through the origin.

misconceptions.question: What is a newtonmeter used to measure?
misconceptions.correct: It measures weight, and more generally force, in newtons. A newtonmeter is a calibrated spring-balance.
misconceptions.misconception: A newtonmeter measures mass in kilograms, in the same way as a set of scales.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The instrument is used in lessons about mass and weight together, and any device that something is hung from is assumed to give a mass reading.
misconceptions.correction: Look at the scale on the instrument. A newtonmeter is marked in newtons because the spring responds to the force pulling on it, which is the weight of the object hung from it.

misconceptions.question: Two forces of 8 N and 3 N act on a box in opposite directions along a line. What is the resultant?
misconceptions.correct: 5 N, in the direction of the 8 N force. Forces acting in opposite directions along a line are subtracted.
misconceptions.misconception: 11 N, because the two forces are added together whatever their directions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Resultant is remembered as 'add the forces up', and the arithmetic is done on the magnitudes without the directions being considered.
misconceptions.correction: Take direction into account before adding. Choose one direction as positive, give the opposing force a negative sign, and add; the resultant then carries both a magnitude and a direction.

misconceptions.question: If two forces act on an object in opposite directions, is the resultant just the larger force?
misconceptions.correct: No. The resultant is the difference between them, acting in the direction of the larger force, and it is zero when they are equal.
misconceptions.misconception: The larger force wins outright, so the resultant is equal to the larger of the two forces.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Tug-of-war language, in which the stronger side wins, encourages the idea that the smaller force is beaten rather than that it reduces the overall effect.
misconceptions.correction: Replace 'wins' with 'reduces'. The smaller force takes away from the larger one, so the single force with the same effect is smaller than the larger force acting alone.

misconceptions.question: Which forces belong on a free body diagram of a box being pulled along the floor?
misconceptions.correct: Only the forces acting on the box: its weight, the normal contact force from the floor, the tension in the rope and friction from the floor.
misconceptions.misconception: The forces the box exerts on other objects, such as its push down on the floor, should be drawn on the same diagram.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Interaction pairs are learned as forces that go together, so students draw both members of each pair even though only one of them acts on the isolated object.
misconceptions.correction: Isolate the object first. A free body diagram shows one object with only the forces acting on it; the partner force of each pair acts on something else and belongs on that object's diagram.

misconceptions.question: A parachutist falls at a steady speed. What is the resultant force, and what does that mean?
misconceptions.correct: The resultant force is zero. The forces are balanced, but both weight and air resistance are still acting on the parachutist.
misconceptions.misconception: A zero resultant force means that no forces are acting on the parachutist at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'No resultant force' is heard as 'no force', so students conclude that the individual forces must have switched off rather than combined to zero.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the forces and their combined effect separate. Each force is still there and still drawn on the free body diagram; it is only their total effect that is zero.

misconceptions.question: A single force is resolved into two components at right angles to each other. How do the components compare with it?
misconceptions.correct: The two component forces together have exactly the same effect as the single force they replace.
misconceptions.misconception: The two components add up numerically to the size of the original force, so a 5 N force gives components of 3 N and 2 N.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Resolving is treated as splitting a quantity like a length of string, so the magnitudes are expected to share out arithmetically.
misconceptions.correction: Remember that components act in different directions, so their magnitudes cannot simply be added. Drawn to scale, components of 3 N and 4 N at right angles replace a single force of 5 N, not 7 N.

misconceptions.question: You have found the resultant of two forces by scale drawing. What must the answer include?
misconceptions.correct: Both the magnitude, measured from the length of the closing arrow using the scale, and the direction, measured with a protractor.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the magnitude in newtons is needed, because that is the number the question is asking for.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Practice with forces in a straight line lets a bare number stand as a complete answer, and the habit survives into vector diagram work where it no longer does.
misconceptions.correction: Force is a vector, so an answer without a direction is incomplete. A scale drawing supplies both parts: measure the arrow for the magnitude and the angle for the direction.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes a scalar quantity?

options.text: It is described by a magnitude only, and never by a direction.
options.rationale: Scalar quantities have magnitude only, which is exactly what this states.

options.text: It is described by a magnitude and also by a direction.
options.rationale: This is the definition of a vector quantity, chosen by students who swap the two terms.

options.text: It is described by a direction, with no size attached.
options.rationale: Students who remember that direction is the key word, but not which term owns it, invert the definition.

options.text: It is described by an arrow that can be any length.
options.rationale: The arrow representation is remembered from the same page of notes and attached to the wrong term.

mcqs.stem: Which statement is true of a vector quantity but not of a scalar quantity?

options.text: It can be given a size in a unit such as the newton.
options.rationale: Being able to state a size is common to both, so a student who thinks a magnitude alone describes a force picks it.

options.text: It always describes an object that is moving.
options.rationale: Vectors are tied to motion, but weight is a vector and a stationary object still has one.

options.text: It can be shown as a label on a scale diagram.
options.rationale: Any quantity can be labelled on a diagram; the arrow is a representation, not the defining property.

options.text: It has a direction associated with its magnitude.
options.rationale: Vector quantities have magnitude and an associated direction, and that direction is what a scalar lacks.

mcqs.stem: Two forces are drawn as arrows on the same diagram. One arrow is twice as long as the other. What does this tell you?

options.text: The two forces are equal, but drawn at two different scales.
options.rationale: On one diagram a single scale is used, so different lengths must mean different magnitudes.

options.text: The longer arrow shows a force acting for twice as long.
options.rationale: Arrow length is read as a duration, but the length of the arrow represents the magnitude, not a time.

options.text: The force shown by the longer arrow is twice as large.
options.rationale: The length of the arrow represents the magnitude, so a doubled length is a doubled force.

options.text: The longer arrow shows the force acting in reverse.
options.rationale: Direction is shown by the way the arrow points, not by how long it is drawn.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes what a force is?

options.text: A property of an object that heavy objects have more of.
options.rationale: Force is treated as a possession of the object rather than as an interaction between two objects.

options.text: Something stored in a moving object and used up later.
options.rationale: This confuses force with a store of energy that the object carries around with it.

options.text: A push or pull that acts only when two objects touch.
options.rationale: Contact forces are the visible ones, so the whole definition is narrowed to touching objects.

options.text: A push or pull on an object due to another object.
options.rationale: A force is a push or pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object.

mcqs.stem: A crate is dragged across a rough floor. Why is the friction between the crate and the floor a contact force?

options.text: Because friction always acts to slow a moving object down.
options.rationale: This describes what friction does, not why it is classified as a contact force.

options.text: Because the crate is also touching the air around it.
options.rationale: The classification is set by the two objects the force acts between, which here are the crate and the floor.

options.text: Because the crate and the floor are physically touching.
options.rationale: Contact forces are those where the objects are physically touching, which the crate and floor are.

options.text: Because the crate rests on the ground, not falling.
options.rationale: Students judge by the situation the object is in rather than by which objects the force acts between.

mcqs.stem: The Earth pulls on a satellite high above its surface. Why is this gravitational force a non-contact force?

options.text: Because there is no air in space to pass the force along.
options.rationale: A medium is not needed; the classification depends only on whether the two objects touch.

options.text: Because the Earth and the satellite are physically separated.
options.rationale: Non-contact forces act between objects that are physically separated, which is the case here.

options.text: Because the two objects can never touch one another.
options.rationale: Whether the objects could touch is irrelevant; magnets are non-contact even when stuck together.

options.text: Because gravity gets weaker as the distance grows.
options.rationale: The strength of the force does change with distance, but that is not what makes it non-contact.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an example of a contact force?

options.text: The tension in a stretched tow-rope
options.rationale: Tension is listed by the specification as a contact force, alongside friction and air resistance.

options.text: The magnetic force between two bar magnets
options.rationale: Magnetic force is non-contact. It acts across a gap and stays non-contact even when the magnets touch.

options.text: The gravitational force on a falling ball
options.rationale: Gravitational force acts between the Earth and the ball, which are physically separated.

options.text: The electrostatic force between charges
options.rationale: Electrostatic force acts across the gap between charged objects, so it is non-contact.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an example of a non-contact force?

options.text: The air resistance on a falling skydiver
options.rationale: Air resistance is a contact force: the skydiver is touching the particles of the air.

options.text: The normal contact force from a table top
options.rationale: The table and the object on it are physically touching, so this force is a contact force.

options.text: The friction between a tyre and a road
options.rationale: Friction acts between two touching surfaces, so it is a contact force.

options.text: The electrostatic force between charges
options.rationale: Electrostatic force is listed by the specification as a non-contact force.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of forces are both non-contact forces?

options.text: Magnetic and gravitational forces
options.rationale: Both are listed by the specification as non-contact forces, acting between separated objects.

options.text: Air resistance and electrostatic force
options.rationale: Electrostatic force is non-contact, but air resistance is a contact force with the air particles.

options.text: Friction and the normal contact force
options.rationale: Both of these are contact forces, so the pair is the opposite of what was asked for.

options.text: Tension and the magnetic force
options.rationale: Magnetic force is non-contact, but tension acts along a rope that is touching the object.

mcqs.stem: A student writes that the force on a trolley is 12 N. Why is this description incomplete?

options.text: Because the mass of the trolley has not been given as well.
options.rationale: The mass is not part of the description of a force; the missing item is the direction.

options.text: Because force is a vector, so a direction is needed.
options.rationale: Force is a vector quantity, so a full description gives the magnitude and the direction.

options.text: Because a force in newtons must be converted to kilograms.
options.rationale: Newtons are the correct unit for force; kilograms are the unit for mass.

options.text: Because a scalar quantity is never written with a unit.
options.rationale: Scalars are written with units too, and force is a vector rather than a scalar.

mcqs.stem: A tennis ball is struck by a racket. Which statement describes the interaction between them correctly?

options.text: Only the racket exerts a force, because it moved first of all.
options.rationale: An interaction always produces a force on each object; a single one-sided force is not possible.

options.text: The racket pushes the ball harder than the ball pushes the racket.
options.rationale: The unequal effect on the two objects is read as evidence of unequal forces.

options.text: Each exerts a force on the other, equal in size and opposite in direction.
options.rationale: The two objects interact, and the interaction produces a force on each of them, drawn as a pair of vectors.

options.text: Both forces act on the ball, so they cancel and it cannot move.
options.rationale: The two forces of an interaction pair act on different objects, so they can never cancel.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the weight of a book resting on a shelf is correct?

options.text: It is the total amount of matter contained in the book.
options.rationale: This describes mass, which is measured in kilograms and is not a force.

options.text: It is the push of the shelf upwards on the book.
options.rationale: That upward push is the normal contact force from the shelf, not the weight of the book.

options.text: It is a property the book has whatever happens.
options.rationale: Mass is unchanged by location, but weight depends on the gravitational field strength there.

options.text: It is the force acting on the book due to gravity.
options.rationale: Weight is the force acting on an object due to gravity, which close to the Earth is due to its gravitational field.

mcqs.stem: An astronaut takes a 3 kg toolbox from the Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg) to the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg). What happens?

options.text: Its mass and weight both fall, because gravity is weaker there.
options.rationale: Anything that reduces the weight is assumed to reduce the mass as well, because the two are merged.

options.text: Its weight stays the same but its mass becomes smaller there.
options.rationale: The two quantities are correctly seen as different, but their roles have been swapped over.

options.text: Its mass stays at 3 kg but its weight becomes smaller.
options.rationale: Mass does not depend on location; weight depends on the gravitational field strength at that point.

options.text: Its mass and its weight do not change on the way there.
options.rationale: Weight is treated as a fixed property, when it depends on the field strength where the object is.

mcqs.stem: Which equation is used to calculate the weight of an object?

options.text: weight = mass ÷ the gravitational field strength
options.rationale: The relationship is remembered as a division, which is the rearrangement used for finding mass.

options.text: weight = mass plus gravitational field strength
options.rationale: The quantities are combined by whichever operation is recalled first, giving a quantity that is not a force.

options.text: weight = gravitational field strength g ÷ mass
options.rationale: The two quantities are divided the wrong way round.

options.text: weight = mass × gravitational field strength
options.rationale: This is the equation exactly as the specification gives it, W = m g.

mcqs.stem: A rock has a mass of 12 kg. The gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the weight of the rock?

options.rationale: The mass and the field strength have been added instead of multiplied.
The mass in kilograms is copied out as though it were the weight in newtons.
The mass has been divided by roughly ten, treating g as a divisor rather than a multiplier.
W = m g = 12 × 9.8 = 117.6 N, with weight in newtons.

mcqs.stem: A bag has a weight of 49 N at a place where the gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the mass of the bag?

options.text: 5 kg
options.rationale: Rearranging W = m g gives m = W ÷ g = 49 ÷ 9.8 = 5 kg.
The weight has been multiplied by g instead of divided by it.
The weight and the field strength have been added together.

options.text: 0.2 kg
options.rationale: The division has been done the wrong way round, giving g ÷ W.

mcqs.stem: Which row gives the correct units for the quantities in W = m g?

options.text: W in newtons, m in kilograms and g in newtons per kilogram
options.rationale: These are the units exactly as the specification gives them: N, kg and N/kg.

options.text: W in kilograms, m in kilograms and g in newtons per kilogram
options.rationale: Weight is given the unit of mass, the usual sign of merging the two quantities.

options.text: W in grams, m in kilograms and g in newtons per kilogram
options.rationale: Weight is again treated as a mass, this time in the unit used on food packaging.

options.text: W in newtons, m in kilograms and g in newtons of force
options.rationale: The field strength is treated as a force, so it is given the unit of a force.

mcqs.stem: What does g stand for in the equation W = m g, and what is its unit?

options.text: Gravitational field strength, measured in newtons per kilogram
options.rationale: The specification gives gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg.

options.text: The force of gravity acting on the object, given in newtons
options.rationale: The symbol is spoken as 'gravity', so it is taken to be the force itself rather than the field strength.

options.text: The mass of the object, which is measured in kilograms
options.rationale: The two symbols in the equation are confused, which would leave the mass counted twice.

options.text: The strength of gravity there, measured in kilograms
options.rationale: A vague idea of 'gravity' is given the unit that the student associates with heaviness.

mcqs.stem: Why is the weight of an object drawn as a single arrow from one point on it?

options.text: Because weight acts where the object presses on the surface below.
options.rationale: The effect of weight is felt at the contact with the ground, so the force is drawn there instead.

options.text: Because the weight may be taken to act at the centre of mass.
options.rationale: The weight of an object may be considered to act at a single point, its centre of mass.

options.text: Because only the heaviest part of an object is pulled by gravity.
options.rationale: Gravity acts on the whole object; the single point is a way of representing that pull.

options.text: Because a vector must always be drawn from the ground.
options.rationale: There is no such rule; where the arrow starts shows where the force is taken to act.

mcqs.stem: The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional. What does this mean?

options.text: Weight increases by a fixed amount each time mass increases.
options.rationale: Proportionality is read as adding on the same amount rather than as multiplying by the same number.

options.text: Doubling the mass doubles the weight in the same field.
options.rationale: Directly proportional means one quantity is a fixed multiple of the other, so the factor carries across.

options.text: Weight becomes smaller as the mass of an object grows.
options.rationale: Direct proportion has been confused with an inverse relationship.

options.text: Weight and mass are equal when the units are ignored.
options.rationale: Proportional is taken to mean identical, which merges the two quantities.

mcqs.stem: A block of mass 4 kg has a weight of 24 N on a planet. A second block on the same planet has a mass of 12 kg. What is its weight?

options.text: 32 N, because the extra 8 kg of mass adds another 8 N to the weight.
options.rationale: Proportionality is applied as an addition, so each extra kilogram is taken to add one newton.

options.text: 72 N, because the mass is three times larger and so the weight is too.
options.rationale: Weight and mass are directly proportional, so a mass three times larger gives a weight three times larger.

options.text: 8 N, because the larger mass is divided by the first weight found.
options.rationale: The numbers are divided rather than scaled, giving a value smaller than the original weight.

options.text: 36 N, because the weight goes up by 12 N for each extra block.
options.rationale: A fixed step is invented instead of using the ratio between mass and weight.

mcqs.stem: Which instrument is used to measure the weight of an object?

options.text: A set of kitchen scales marked in kilograms
options.rationale: Scales marked in kilograms give a mass, not a weight in newtons.

options.text: An electronic balance reading in kilograms
options.rationale: This also reads a mass; no force in newtons is measured by it.

options.text: A spring-balance calibrated in newtons
options.rationale: Weight is measured using a calibrated spring-balance, also called a newtonmeter.

options.text: A balance comparing two known masses
options.rationale: A balance compares masses, which is a different quantity from weight.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the resultant force on an object?

options.text: The largest of all of the forces that are acting on the object.
options.rationale: The biggest force is treated as the one that wins, rather than being combined with the others.

options.text: The force that is left once the object has stopped moving.
options.rationale: Resultant force is tied to the motion of the object rather than to combining the forces.

options.text: The single force with the same effect as all of them together.
options.rationale: A number of forces may be replaced by a single force with the same effect: the resultant force.

options.text: The total of the sizes of every force that acts on it.
options.rationale: Magnitudes are added with no regard to direction, which overstates opposing forces.

mcqs.stem: A box is pulled to the right with a force of 12 N while a friction force of 5 N acts to the left. What is the resultant force?

options.text: 17 N, acting to the right
options.rationale: The two magnitudes have been added even though the forces act in opposite directions.

options.text: 12 N acting to the right
options.rationale: The larger force is taken to win outright, so the friction force is ignored.

options.text: 7 N acting to the left
options.rationale: The subtraction is right but the resultant is given the direction of the smaller force.

options.text: 7 N acting to the right
options.rationale: For forces in a straight line the resultant is 12 - 5 = 7 N, in the direction of the larger force.

mcqs.stem: A ball hangs at rest on the end of a string. A free body diagram of the ball is drawn. Which forces should appear on it?

options.text: The tension in the string and the pull of the ball on the string as well.
options.rationale: Both members of the interaction pair are drawn, although one of them acts on the string.

options.text: The weight of the ball and the pull of the ball on the Earth below.
options.rationale: The partner force acts on the Earth, so it belongs on a diagram of the Earth instead.

options.text: The weight of the ball and the tension in the string, both acting on the ball.
options.rationale: A free body diagram shows the isolated object with only the forces that act on it.

options.text: No forces at all, because the ball is hanging still on the string.
options.rationale: A stationary object is assumed to have no forces on it, rather than balanced forces.

mcqs.stem: A parachutist falls at a steady speed. Her weight is 700 N. What can be said about the forces on her?

options.text: Air resistance is larger than her weight, so the resultant is upwards.
options.rationale: A larger upward force is assumed to be needed, but that would make her slow down.

options.text: Air resistance is 700 N upwards, so the resultant force is zero.
options.rationale: The forces are balanced: an upward 700 N air resistance and a 700 N weight give a resultant of zero.

options.text: Her weight has fallen to zero, leaving air resistance only.
options.rationale: Weight is treated as something that disappears once the motion becomes steady.

options.text: No forces act on her now, since her speed is not changing.
options.rationale: A zero resultant is heard as 'no forces', so the individual forces are taken to have switched off.

mcqs.stem: A single force is resolved into two components acting at right angles to each other. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The two components together have the same effect as the force.
options.rationale: The two component forces together have the same effect as the single force they replace.

options.text: The two components add up numerically to the size of the single force.
options.rationale: Resolving is treated as sharing out a quantity, so the magnitudes are expected to add.

options.text: Each component is exactly half the size of the original single force.
options.rationale: The force is assumed to be split evenly, which is only ever true in one special case.

options.text: The two components replace a force that has no direction.
options.rationale: The original force is a vector; it is precisely its direction that makes resolving useful.

mcqs.stem: Two forces at right angles act on a point. A student draws them to scale, head to tail, to find the resultant. What must the final answer state?

options.text: The magnitude in newtons only, since that is the number asked for.
options.rationale: A bare number is accepted as complete, as it can be for forces acting in a straight line.

options.text: The magnitude in newtons and the direction of the force.
options.rationale: The resultant is a vector, so the answer gives both magnitude and direction from the scale drawing.

options.text: The direction only, because a scale drawing cannot give a size.
options.rationale: A scale drawing gives both: the closing arrow is measured and converted using the stated scale.

options.text: The magnitude in newtons and the total length of both arrows.
options.rationale: The lengths of the drawn arrows are the working, not part of the answer itself.
